Québec supprime deux programmes de souti: Quebec cuts two support programs for women who are victims of domestic violence
Le 31 mars marquera la fin officielle du: March 31 will mark the official end of the interpretation service for immigrant women who are victims of sexual and domestic violence.

March 31 will mark the official end of the interpretation service for immigrant women who are victims of sexual and domestic violence. Launched in 2020, this essential service had already nearly disappeared in March 2024, before being extended for a year at the last minute. Now it is being abandoned for good.
Un véritable coup dur pour les femmes vi: It is a real blow for women who are victims of violence and for the community organizations that support them. The decision comes only a few months after another major setback: the end of Phase II of the <l1>Rebâtir</l1> project last September. That program allowed women to access specialized legal representation when an abusive partner used strategies to keep the victim from getting a lawyer. It was an essential protection, given that some perpetrators contact lawyers before their partners do, to keep them from being represented.
Des choix politiques décriés par les org: These political choices, decried by victim support organizations, give the impression of a clear step backward for women’s rights, and this is still Women’s Rights Month.
<strong>Tandis que 60 femmes ont été tué: While 60 women have been killed by their spouse or ex-partner in Quebec since 2020, 13 of them last year, the provincial government has ended two programs that help victims of domestic violence. The news has sent a shockwave through survivors and advocates for women who are victims of physical, sexual or psychological violence. Here is what’s going on.
« On dirait qu’on déconstruit morceau pa: “It feels like the things that were put in place to help women who are victims of violence are being dismantled piece by piece. It’s pretty troubling to see that we move forward, and then we take a step back,” says Louise Riendeau of the Regroupement des maisons pour femmes victimes de violence conjugale. Like her, several representatives of community organizations that support women victims of violence say they don’t understand. They are denouncing the end of two government programs in Quebec, even though the fight against violence against women is presented by the government as a priority.
Pourtant, au Canada, on dénombrait en 20: Yet in Canada in 2022, there were nearly 120,000 victims of intimate partner violence (IPV) among people over the age of 12, 78% of them women or girls. According to Statistics Canada, this scourge grew by 163% between 2014 and 2022. But that is only the visible tip of the iceberg, since an estimated 80% of IPV is not reported to police and is therefore not counted. The real number of people victimized by their partners is much higher.
Prises dans le cycle de la violence, les: Caught in the cycle of violence, survivors often need time, and several attempts, to get away before it’s too late. Then a second battle begins: rebuilding. Broken and isolated, these women suffer from post-traumatic stress, have lost their homes, sometimes have children. They are extremely vulnerable and need help.
S’amorce alors un cheminement – au cours: A journey begins, but along the way they will no longer have access to two government programs that specialized organizations describe as particularly necessary. The first ended in September 2024 and was part of the <l1>Rebâtir</l1> pilot project, launched in 2021. It allowed women to be represented by a specialized lawyer in cases of conflict of interest. One strategy used by some perpetrators to keep their partner from hiring a lawyer is to contact dozens of lawyers before she does. Under their code of ethics, lawyers who have been contacted by one party cannot agree to represent the other. The Rebâtir telephone line, which has offered four hours of free legal consultation to victims of domestic or sexual violence since 2021, remains in service.
Le second programme permet aux femmes im: The second program allows immigrant women who are victims of IPV to use the services of an interpreter when they are not comfortable enough in French or English. Launched in 2020, it had already been under threat in March 2024 but was renewed for one year. That reprieve ends on March 31.
<strong>« Il ne suffit pas juste de trad: “It’s not enough to just translate like Google Translate!”
« De janvier 2024 à mars 2025, 35 interp: “From January 2024 to March 2025, 35 interpreters were called on 88 times to work in domestic violence situations,” Emmanuel Siake Nganka tells us. He is in charge of the interpreter bank at the Maison Internationale, an organization that welcomes thousands of people each year.
À la fin du mois, il ne sera plus possib: At the end of the month, the organizations that support these women will no longer be able to use an interpreter’s services free of charge. Front-line workers fear they will have to fall back on cheaper methods that could prove dangerous for victims.
« Les personnes qu’on accompagne, ce ne: “The people we support aren’t numbers. They’re people we follow over the long term. We welcome people from different parts of the world: Latin America, Central Africa, the Middle East, Syria, Iraq, Afghanistan, Pakistan. Among them are women who are victims of domestic violence and speak neither French nor English,” begins Mame Moussa Sy, the organization’s executive director, visibly irritated.
« Les interprètes financés par le MIFI [: “The interpreters funded by the MIFI [Editor’s note: Quebec’s Ministry of Immigration, Francization and Integration] have specific training on what these women go through. It’s not enough to just translate like Google Translate! There’s also the intercultural dimension, because words don’t mean the same thing everywhere,” Mame Moussa Sy continues.
Comment ces personnes fragilisées pourro: How will these vulnerable people be able to tell what they are going through if they don’t have the words? “We’ll manage,” the executive director sighs. “We’ll ask a cousin, a neighbour to translate, but looking for a free option in this kind of case is dangerous. A relative can break confidentiality, intentionally or not. There’s also a conflict of interest, because in some cultures, a woman who wants to leave the home is frowned upon, and a translator who isn’t neutral can distort the message so that she stays with her husband,” he points out.
Un constat que fait également Amina Naja: Amina Najat, an interpreter of Dari, a language spoken in Afghanistan, and Urdu, the language of Pakistan, where she lived for about fifteen years, sees it the same way.
<strong>Pour ces femmes, savoir qu’on pa: For these women, knowing someone speaks their language is a relief
« Parfois les interprètes sont les premi: “Sometimes interpreters are the first people these women speak to freely,” she explains. She recalls one mother, a victim of domestic violence, for whom she interpreted: “This woman only spoke her mother tongue. She was controlled by her husband, isolated, with no support at all. She didn’t even know how to take the bus alone,” she says.
Très religieuse, la victime était confro: Deeply religious, the victim faced a profound dilemma: “She didn’t know what to do: ‘Who do I listen to? My husband? My family? My parents, who encourage me to stay with my husband? Or my children, who keep telling me: “You’ve already put up with so much, you can keep going.”’ No one around her saw leaving as an option. There’s a real culture of silence,” the interpreter continues. “Women are taught to say nothing, to keep everything to themselves. Even talking to a friend carries a risk: that the story spreads.”
Au fil des rencontres, la victime a pu m: Over the course of their meetings, the victim was able to put words to what she was feeling, understand her rights and discover the resources available to her. “It wasn’t a magical transformation, but little by little, she regained confidence, she learned to set her limits. I also explained the differences between her culture of origin and Quebec’s, particularly when it comes to women’s rights.”
L’histoire de cette femme n’est pas une: This woman’s story is not an exception, Amina says. It is a path many victims take. They keep their suffering quiet and stifle their emotions. But when they speak to a professional interpreter, they often manage for the first time to express what they are living through, without fear of being judged. “For these women, knowing someone speaks their language is a relief. They no longer have to try to translate their pain into a language they don’t master. It’s one less mental burden. And everything starts with speaking.”
Les conséquences de la fin du programme: The consequences of ending the interpreter program will be dramatic, Amina warns: “Some women will never speak up. They will keep suffering. In fact, they think they’ve only changed countries, but that their fate stays the same. Some even tell themselves that what they’re going through is their own fault: ‘I’ve been punished, I’m the one who chose the wrong husband.’”
L’interprète rappelle que l’intégration: The interpreter points out that these immigrant women’s integration into their host country also depends on access to their rights. “Here, there’s a lot of emphasis on feminism and on the duty to integrate. Learning the language is good, but in the meantime, how are they supposed to survive? We talk about feminism, but we abandon these women… And their children suffer the consequences. These patterns of violence are passed down from generation to generation.”
Alors que les discours politiques metten: While political speeches stress the fight against violence against women, the elimination of the interpretation service is a paradox that leaves in the shadows those who already have no voice.
Interrogé par La Converse, le ministère: Asked by La Converse, the Ministère de l’Immigration, de la Francisation et de l’Intégration (MIFI) explained its decision: “Interpretation and translation activities for public services have no longer been eligible under the standards of the Programme d’appui aux collectivités (PAC) since those standards were revised in 2023. The project is not eligible under the MIFI’s other standardized programs, notably the Programme d’accueil et de soutien à l’intégration (PASI). The organization was informed on March 7 that its funding would not be renewed.” The ministry is thus presenting it as a choice made by default.
<strong>Seule et prise dans un engrenage: Alone and caught in an endless legal battle
En 2017, Caroline se sépare de son conjo: In 2017, Caroline separated from her partner. On paper, the divorce was supposed to be amicable, but it turned into a long and gruelling legal fight. “He never accepted the separation,” she confides. She quickly ran into a series of obstacles: refusal to cooperate, various forms of manipulation, relentlessness, deliberately drawn-out court proceedings. “During negotiations, he made completely outlandish demands that led to endless legal proceedings,” she continues, “not to mention the many impacts on the children.” For four years, she dealt with her ex-partner’s manoeuvres. Beyond the personal toll, a real legal war began.
Caroline doit faire face à ce qu’elle qu: Caroline had to deal with what she calls “judicial violence,” a strategy her ex-partner used to slow down the proceedings and wear her out. “Financially, it crippled me like you wouldn’t believe,” she confides, mentioning the tens of thousands of dollars spent on legal fees. Her own lawyer was once astonished at the situation: “She told me she’d never seen anything like it in her career.”
Caroline raconte avec lassitude les tact: Caroline wearily describes the tactics her ex-husband used to drag things out: “At one point, he no longer had a lawyer, so he was communicating with my lawyer, and she was obliged to answer him, to take the time to explain things… But he kept asking the same questions in different forms. And all that time, I was the one paying the lawyer, and the bill kept climbing.”
Après des années de lutte, un nouvel obs: After years of struggle, a new obstacle appeared: her lawyer retired. Caroline found herself without legal representation, in a case that had become so complex that no lawyer would take it on. Out of resources, and deprived of thousands of dollars in unpaid child support, Caroline could not give up. If she couldn’t afford a lawyer, she would represent herself. “I wanted a trial date to conclude this saga and have a judge rule once and for all on everything he had been so relentless about. I also wanted to see the money owed to my children released,” she explains.
Dans cette épreuve, elle trouve du souti: Through this ordeal, she found support from the organization Rebâtir, which helped her structure her case and prepare her defence. She praises the help of its lawyers: “Me Lacroix gave me confidence in my ability to represent myself.” Through the program, she received four hours of free consultation for domestic violence, plus four additional hours after sexual violence was recognized. “With the email exchanges, I probably got about 10 hours in total,” she says. It was valuable help, but not enough given the scale of the task.
Les dossiers judiciaires de Caroline, do: Caroline’s court files, with the documents meticulously sorted. Photo: courtesy of Caroline
« Dix heures, c’est vite passé quand il: “Ten hours goes fast when you have to build an entire case. I was lucky to have already had a lawyer before, so I understood the system a bit better. But it’s still stressful to represent yourself in court. You don’t know when to speak, how to phrase things, what to object to… And you don’t want to come across as the crazy woman who opposes everything,” she confides. Rebâtir helped her refocus and stay relevant in her interventions.
Pendant un mois, celle qui est intervena: For a month, the social worker set her job aside to prepare for her trial. She gathered hundreds of documents, sorted her evidence into several volumes and refined her arguments. It was a titanic effort that finally paid off: although her trial was scheduled to last two days, she won her case on the first day. It was an immense relief after four years of fighting.
Lorsqu’on lui demande pourquoi elle n’a: When asked why she didn’t choose to be represented by a Rebâtir lawyer, she exclaims: “Oh? I could have been represented? If I’d known I had that option, obviously I would have taken it!” She pauses. “I don’t know why it wasn’t offered to me… Maybe my case was too far along? I have no idea.”
Malgré tout, Caroline est fière d’avoir: Still, Caroline is proud to have succeeded on her own. “It’s an enormous reclaiming of power over my life,” she says. But she doesn’t hide that it was a gigantic ordeal: “Going to court and facing, alone, the person who put me through so many horrors… It takes immense courage.”
Un paradoxe apparaît ici : ce programme: A paradox emerges here: this legal representation program was abolished, officially because of a lack of demand. Caroline, a mother of two teenagers, like so many others, simply didn’t know it existed. Access to justice isn’t just about resources; victims also have to know about them.
<strong>Rebâtir : « On aurait souhaité q: Rebâtir: “We would have liked it to be expanded across all of Quebec, rather than cut”
« La Commission des services juridiques: “The Commission des services juridiques says there aren’t many conflict-of-interest cases, so [Phase II of the Rebâtir project] wasn’t necessary, except that they still represented a few hundred victims and that service was very much appreciated,” begins Louise Riendeau by videoconference, joined by Justine Fortin. Both are in charge of policy files at the Regroupement des maisons pour femmes victimes de violence conjugale.
En un an, les avocats du projet Rebâtir: In one year, the Rebâtir project’s lawyers provided legal assistance in 190 cases of intimate partner violence. But according to the Commission des services juridiques (CSJ), the body responsible for applying the Legal Aid Act, conflict-of-interest cases account for 14% of files. Quebec judged that need to be insufficient, according to information from Le Devoir.
Pourtant, face à des conjoints qui explo: Yet when partners exploit every loophole in the legal system to maintain their hold over their ex, the need persists: “When you’re a victim of domestic violence, your rights are already being violated, you’re already in an unfair situation. So you need to be represented by a competent lawyer to help rebalance rights, wealth and custody-sharing. With the end of Phase II of Rebâtir, these women risk having no one left to defend their rights,” Justine Fortin insists.
« On aurait souhaité qu’il soit élargi à: “We would have liked it to be expanded across all of Quebec, rather than cut,” Louise Riendeau argues. The program was limited to Montréal, the Montérégie and Quebec City. The two women believe the need is even greater outside major centres. “In many regions, women find themselves without a lawyer, with no callback from legal aid, and have to make do with a list of private lawyers who, all too often, don’t take cases,” M<sup>s</sup>. Riendeau insists.
<strong>Un groupe Facebook pour pallier: A Facebook group to fill the gap in resources for victims
Mariana Infante, qui a quitté son Mexiqu: Mariana Infante, who left her native Mexico to <l1>flee her ex-husband’s violence</l1>, says she is “shocked” by the end of these programs. “I find it really unfair and I don’t understand how this is possible,” she protests. “As women, we’re already a vulnerable group, and we see every day that our rights are never guaranteed and that we have to fight to keep them from being taken away. When you’re a woman and you’re experiencing violence, you’re even more vulnerable.”
La mère de famille regrette aussi le fai: The mother also regrets that survivors know so little about the resources available: “I didn’t even know the Rebâtir program gave access to a specialized lawyer in cases of conflict of interest, and I work with an organization for women. I know a lot of women who would have needed this service. So, to say they’re not continuing it because there isn’t enough demand, I find that unfair.”
Mariana a conscience du manque criant de: Mariana is acutely aware of the lack of resources and communication for victims, having gone down that painful road herself. That is why she created a Facebook group a few years ago. “So far, there are 200 members, because it’s a private group… You have to prove your profile is real. If someone sends a request, we have to meet that person in person to verify their identity, because it has happened that abusive partners created fake profiles to get into the group,” she adds.
Au sein de ce groupe virtuel, des travai: In this virtual group, social workers, lawyers, psychologists and interpreters answer women’s questions and support them in their efforts on a volunteer basis. “Some legal aid lawyers have a lot of prejudices and aren’t trained on partner violence issues. Several women have the door slammed in their faces because they went to the lawyer once, but went back to their husband for all kinds of reasons. When they finally come back, some lawyers say: ‘Listen, ma’am, I took your case a long time ago. You left without saying anything, and now you’re telling me you want a divorce.’ So even though it’s a right, they end up without a lawyer at the worst possible time,” Mariana points out.
Grâce au groupe Facebook et au réseau de: Thanks to the Facebook group and the support network Mariana created, these women find help and are directed to the right people, professionals who are committed to supporting them. Of course, Mariana Infante would prefer that this group didn’t exist, like all the other citizen initiatives that make up for the poor handling of these victims’ needs. “If they keep shutting down programs like these two, we’ll have to keep doing what we’re doing, unfortunately, and that’s worrying for our society,” she concludes.
